title: Park, Gym, Lights
bigQuestion: Who pays for the parks, gyms and lighted fields where a town plays?

story.title: Lights Before the Crowd
story.kicker: Friday lights click on over an empty field before anyone arrives.
paragraphs: It is Friday. The sun goes down behind a high school. The field is empty. Then tall poles click on. The grass turns bright green.
Nobody has come yet. But somebody already paid for this field. The town paid for the grass. The school district paid for the poles and the bulbs.
Soon cars will park. Families will fill the bleachers. They did not each buy a field. They share one field that the whole town paid for.
A place like this is a civic place. Civic means it belongs to the people of a town. Parks and school gyms are civic places too.
story.think: Who do you think paid for the park or gym closest to your school?

lessons.title: Lincoln Park Gets Its Name
lessons.mainIdea: Chicago turned old city land into Lincoln Park, a park for everyone.
reading: Lincoln Park sits by Lake Michigan in Chicago. Long ago, part of this land was a city cemetery. Chicago moved the graves and made a park.
In 1865, the city named it Lincoln Park. That year, President Abraham Lincoln had died. A *public park* is open to everyone in town.

words.d: land a city keeps open so everyone can use it

look.title: From Cemetery to Park
look.text: Part of Lincoln Park began as Chicago's City Cemetery. The city moved the graves and renamed the park after Abraham Lincoln in 1865.
look.cite: Chicago Park District, history of Lincoln Park
look.prompt: What was part of this land before it was a park?

check.q: Whose name did Chicago give the park in 1865?
check.why: The city named the park for President Abraham Lincoln in 1865.

check.q: What was part of the land before the park?
check.why: Part of the land was Chicago's City Cemetery. The graves were moved.

check.q: Who may use a public park?
check.why: A public park is open to everyone.

lessons.title: Small Parks With Field Houses
lessons.mainIdea: In 1905, Chicago opened small parks with field houses near homes.
reading: Many Chicago children lived in crowded blocks. Big parks were far away. In 1905, the South Side opened small parks close to homes.
Each park had a *field house*. It held a gym, showers and meeting rooms. Families could walk there. Later, in 1934, Chicago joined its park groups into one Chicago Park District.

words.d: a building in a park with a gym and rooms for the neighborhood
a local public group that runs parks and park buildings

choices: Big parks were far from many children.
check.why: Children in crowded blocks lived far from big parks.

choices: a park building with a gym and rooms
check.why: A field house held a gym, showers and meeting rooms.

check.q: When did the Chicago Park District form?
check.why: Chicago joined its park groups into one district in 1934.

lessons.title: Who Pays for a School Gym
lessons.mainIdea: A public school gym is paid for with money the whole town shares.
reading: A *school district* runs the public schools in a town. People who live there pay taxes. Some of that tax money builds and fixes schools.
A school board votes on how to spend the money. A new gym needs that vote. The gym holds classes by day and games after school.

words.d: the public group that runs the schools in a town
money people pay to their town or state to pay for shared things

look.title: Two Hoops
look.text: Look at a hoop on a garage in a driveway. One family bought it. Now look at a hoop in a school gym. Many families paid for it with their taxes.
look.prompt: Who may use each hoop? Why is it different?

check.q: Where does some money for a school gym come from?
check.why: People in town pay taxes. Some of it builds schools.

check.q: When is a school gym used?
choices: for classes by day and games after school
check.why: The same room holds classes and after-school games.

lessons.title: Naismith's Winter Gym
lessons.mainIdea: Basketball began in a gym in Springfield, Massachusetts, in December 1891.
reading: James Naismith taught at a YMCA school in Springfield, Massachusetts. Winter was cold. His class could not play outside.
In December 1891, he needed an indoor game. He hung two peach baskets in the *gym*. His class of eighteen men played the first basketball game.

words.d: a large indoor room for exercise and games
Young Men's Christian Association, a group that ran gyms and classes

look.title: A Game for Winter
look.text: Naismith wrote that his class needed a game they could play indoors during the winter months. He used peach baskets as goals.

lessons.title: A Fair Full of Lights
lessons.mainIdea: Chicago's 1893 world's fair showed how electric lights could fill a place at night.
reading: In 1893, Chicago held a giant fair. It was called the World's Columbian Exposition. Millions of people came.
At night, thousands of *electric lights* lit the fair buildings. People could stay after dark. Later, towns used electric lights on fields too.

words.d: a lamp that glows using electricity

look.title: The Fair at Night
look.text: Look at white buildings beside the water. The sky is dark. Rows of lamps glow along every roof. Crowds still walk on the paths.
look.prompt: What could people do at night because of the lights?

check.why: The World's Columbian Exposition was in Chicago.

check.q: What did the lights let people do?
check.why: Electric lights let crowds stay after dark.

check.q: Where did towns later put electric lights?
check.why: Later, towns lit fields so games could go on after dark.

lessons.title: Wrigley Field Gets Lights
lessons.mainIdea: Wrigley Field in Chicago added lights in 1988, so the Cubs could play at night.
reading: Wrigley Field is the home of the Chicago Cubs. For many years, it had no lights. Every Cubs home game was in daytime.
In 1988, lights went up at Wrigley Field. It was the last big-league ballpark to get them. Now fans could come after work or school.

words.d: a place built for baseball games, with a field and seats
